say: Shapes have secrets. Today we find them by cutting, building and counting. We will count sides and corners, and find shapes hiding inside other shapes.
Shape hunt! In two minutes find a circle, a triangle, a square and a rectangle in the room (at home for online). Bring one of each, or point to them.
I will fold this square corner to corner and cut along the fold. What shapes do you think I will get?
stuck: Stuck: line up the long edges so the shapes touch with no gaps.
Not sure of the name: “Count the sides and the corners. What is the name for 4 sides?”
For pairs who want more: can you make a rectangle? A bigger triangle?

say: “A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners. A square has 4 sides and 4 corners. I notice the number of sides is always the same as the number of corners. So an octagon, with 8 sides, has 8 corners.”
“Counting triangles in this picture: I count the small triangles first: 2. Then I look for a big triangle made of more than one small one: 1. Total 3.”

“In a counting puzzle we can count a square as a special rectangle. Why? It has 4 square corners, like a rectangle. But on the house picture in Q1, a square goes in the Square column only, so we count each shape once.”

do: Ask: “How many sides? How many corners? What do you notice?”
Ask: “Did you count the small triangles first? Now look for the big one.”
Ask: “Which shape am I? I have 4 sides and all are equal.”
stuck: Hint 1: “Trace the shape with your finger and count each side.”
Hint 2: “Colour each small shape a different colour.”
Hint 3: “Count the small shapes first, then the bigger shapes.”

say: “Is a square a rectangle? What makes you say so?”
“How did you make sure you did not miss any triangles?”
ask: “Is a square a rectangle? What makes you say so?”

A square has 4 square corners like a rectangle, so it is a special rectangle. (On the Q1 house picture each shape goes in one column only.) Count small triangles first, then bigger ones made of smaller ones.

say: “You counted in order and explained why a square is also a rectangle. That is careful maths.”

l7-title.note: Objective: Name and describe 2D shapes by sides and corners, count shapes in a picture, count triangles in a figure, and compose shapes. Materials: Paper squares, scissors, pattern blocks, 2 shape riddles on cards. Online: Each child has a paper square to fold and cut on camera; shape hunt at home. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up 2 to 8 (game 2 to 6, quick questions 6 to 8; ask questions 1 to 3, and 4 and 5 only if you are on time), sneak-peek puzzles 8 to 12, explore 12 to 28, teaching 28 to 36 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 36 to 40, worksheet 40 to 72 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it (the last 4 minutes check page 2, after a 1-minute stand-up stretch), talk time 72 to 79, exit ticket 79 to 85, look-back 85 to 88, then flex time and goodbye 88 to 90 (this is the buffer: if you are behind, use it; do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose, any time or at home. Nobody is told which page they should be on.

l7-warm1.note: Minutes 2 to 6. Shape hunt: find a circle, a triangle, a square and a rectangle in the room or at home in 2 minutes.

l7-warm2.note: Minutes 6 to 8. Read each question aloud, give thinking time, take answers, then click to show the answer. Ask "How do you know?" each time. For 4, fold a paper square in front of them after they answer: two rectangles of the same size. Answers: 1) 3 2) 4 3) circle 4) 2 rectangles (if a child says 2 triangles, they folded corner to corner: that is what we do in Explore next). Ask questions 1 to 3. Ask 4 and 5 only if the clock at minute 6 is on time. The 4-minute sneak-peek puzzles follow on the next slide.

l7-warmcheck.note: Minutes 8 to 12 (4 minutes). SAY (about 26 words, once): "Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked." Question 1 is an access question: every child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone starts with a win. Question 2 makes you think. Children try both on their own paper (about a minute each). Then everyone shows their paper ONCE, after the second question: face to face, each child holds the paper low so only the tutor sees it; online, everyone holds the paper to the camera at the same moment. There are no private chat messages. Never use boards held up in front of the group, and never read out or compare anyone's answer. Do not write scores down or announce them. Then click to show each answer to the whole group and say "Lots of us had a different idea, and that is fine." Look for good ideas to praise in a later lesson; do not keep a list of who found question 2 easy. When the worksheet starts (minute 40) invite the WHOLE group (“When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation”), never one child by name. Everyone joins Explore and the Mini-lesson. Answers: 1) 3 sides and 3 corners. 2) 9. A shape has as many straight sides as it has corners.

l7-explore1.note: Minutes 12 to 18. Pairs work with the materials: Paper squares, scissors, pattern blocks, 2 shape riddles on cards. Fold a paper square along a diagonal and cut: what two shapes do you get? Put them together a different way. What new shapes can you make? Online: Each child has a paper square to fold and cut on camera; shape hunt at home. Go further (what-if) is on this slide from the start: any pair may choose it at any time, so nobody waits. The tutor does not choose who and does not announce it. Answers: Two equal rectangles. Put together they can make the square again, a long rectangle or a step shape. Open: accept any correct shape and name.

l7-explore2.note: Minutes 18 to 28. Let pairs keep working and move around the room (or breakout rooms). Gather them to answer these. Answers: 1) Two triangles of the same size. 2) Square, bigger triangle, parallelogram. 3) Square 4, bigger triangle 3, parallelogram 4.

l7-teach1.note: Teach. Ask first: "How many squares can you see?" Most children say 4. Do not correct them yet. Click 1: number the small squares. Click 2: run your finger round the outside: "Is this a square? 4 straight sides, all the same length, 4 square corners. Yes! It is made of 4 small squares." Click 3: 4 + 1 = 5. Click 4: the why. Think-aloud: "Squares can hide inside bigger squares. So I count by size: all the small ones first, then the next size up, then the next. That way I do not miss any and I do not count any twice."

l7-we1.note: Click to reveal each step. Before each click, ask the group to predict. Step 1: count the small squares row by row. Step 2: hold up a paper 2 by 2 window (or cut one from card) and slide it: top left, top right, bottom left, bottom right. "Can it go anywhere else?" No: 4 places. Step 3: the whole grid. Think-aloud: "I count by size. Small squares: 9. Squares 2 across and 2 down: I slide my window, 4 places. Squares 3 across and 3 down: just the whole grid, 1. 9 + 4 + 1 = 14." Watch for children who count squares made of 2 small squares side by side: that shape is a rectangle, not a square.

l7-try1.note: Children write on their own paper and show only the tutor (online: each child holds the paper to the camera at the same moment). Never ask for boards up in front of the group. Then click. a) 3: there is no bigger square, because a bigger square needs 2 rows. b) 6: 5 small squares and 1 square made of 4 small ones (the 2 by 2 part). The extra square cannot make a second big square because the square above it is missing: show this with your 2 by 2 window. c) Open: a 2 by 2 grid (4 + 1) or a row of 5 small squares (5 + 0) both work. Ask a child with each answer to explain.

l7-key.note: Say the key ideas together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Counting only the small shapes: in the triangle-counting pictures (Q4 and the talk-time picture, a square with both lines from corner to corner) children miss the bigger triangles. Ask "Are there bigger triangles made of 2 small ones?" (2) In the house picture (Q1), counting a square window in both the Square and the Rectangle columns. Each shape goes in one column only. (3) Saying a circle has 1 side, or counting the same side twice when going round a shape: put a dot where you start. (4) Thinking a turned or flipped shape is a new one.

l7-break.note: Four minutes. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

l7-teachpic.note: Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q1 counts the shapes in a house picture; this robot is a different picture). Click 1: tick the circles one by one: the two eyes and the button. Click 2: tick the others in a new colour: the hat is a triangle, the head is a square, the mouth, the body and the two feet are rectangles. Click 3: add. Click 4: fill the table. Think-aloud: "If I jump around the picture I will miss one or count one twice. So I pick one kind of shape, find every one and tick it. Then the next kind." Say clearly: a square goes in the Square column only, even though a square is a special rectangle.

l7-teachsides.note: Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q2 is a sides and corners table). Click 1: the start dot. Click 2: trace the outline with your finger and count the sides aloud with the children. Click 3: go round again for the corners (dots). Think-aloud: "This shape has lots of sides, so I could easily lose my place. I put a dot where I start, count each side, and stop when I am back at the dot." Then ask "What do you notice?" but let them test the idea on the worksheet table; do not tell them the rule. The names at the bottom are for Q2: children count the sides of each shape themselves on the worksheet. Memory help: an octopus has 8 arms (octagon).

l7-ws1.note: Minutes 42 to 52. Walk around. Ask "How do you know?" before giving any help. For Q1 check that pairs tick each shape. For Q2 ask "What do you notice about the two numbers?" and "Does it work for every shape?" At minute 40 read questions 1 and 2 aloud, then pairs read the rest. The workbook says: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group; invite the WHOLE group at once, for example: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

l7-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1: the sun is the circle; the roof and the flag are triangles; the 3 windows are squares; the wall and the door are rectangles. 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 8. Q2b: "Each side ends at a corner, and going round, each corner starts the next side, so there are as many corners as sides."

l7-teachwho.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q3 is three "Who am I?" riddles). Read the riddle aloud. Click 1: "Which shapes have 4 corners? Count with me." Cross out the triangle (3), the circle (0), the pentagon (5) and the hexagon (6). Click 2: "Square or rectangle? A square has all sides the same length. My sides are not all the same, so cross out the square." Click 3: check: a rectangle has 4 corners, and its long sides and short sides are different lengths ✓. Think-aloud: "I read one clue at a time and cross out every shape that does not fit. When one shape is left, I check it against every clue."

l7-teachtri.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 asks for the triangles in 3 pictures; this picture is not one of them). Ask first: "How many triangles?" Take guesses. Click through the sizes. Think-aloud: "I count the small triangles first: 1, 2, 3. Now triangles made of 2 small parts: the left two together, the right two together: 2. Then all 3 parts: the whole big triangle: 1. 3 + 2 + 1 = 6." Ask "Is the middle part with the right part a triangle?" Yes. Watch for children who stop after the small ones.

l7-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who may need a short catch-up next lesson (never in front of the group). For Q5, children can use the two triangles they cut in Explore.

l7-ws2ans.note: Click each answer after a child explains. Q4A: 2 small + the whole triangle = 3. Q4B: the line from corner to corner makes 2 triangles; the square is not a triangle. Talk-time picture (square with both lines from corner to corner): 4 small triangles meet in the middle; each line also cuts the square into 2 big triangles, and there are 2 such lines, so 4 big ones: 4 + 4 = 8. Q5: hold up the Explore shapes to check each drawing. First, everyone stands up and stretches for about a minute (reach up high, touch your toes, shake out your hands) so there is some movement before talk time.

l7-stretch.note: For any pair that chooses to try more (these are on the slide only; Think harder T1 to T4 are in the workbook). Answers: 1) 6 (3 single squares, 2 pairs and 1 whole row). 2) 9: 4 small squares, 2 rectangles 2 long lying down, 2 rectangles 2 long standing up, and the whole grid. 3) Yes to both. The 4 triangles make the original square again (corners meeting in the middle), and they also fit together into one big triangle whose long side is twice as long as a small triangle's long side (two along the bottom and two on top).

l7-we2.note: Click to build each length. Say first: "In this puzzle a square counts as a rectangle. Why? A rectangle has 4 square corners and its opposite sides are the same length. A square has all of that too." (On the worksheet's house picture, squares still go only in the Square column.) Think-aloud: "I count by length, shortest first. 1 square long: there are 4. 2 squares long: I slide it along: 3 places. 3 squares long: 2 places. The whole strip: 1. Each time the length goes up by 1, there is one fewer place. 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10." Use a paper strip and a card window to slide along it.

l7-try2.note: Own paper, shown only to the tutor (online: all hold the paper to the camera at the same moment), then click. a) 2 + 1 = 3. b) Slide a 2-long window along 5 squares: it fits in 4 places. c) From the worked example there are 10 rectangles; the 4 single squares are squares, so 10 − 4 = 6 (3 that are 2 long, 2 that are 3 long, 1 that is 4 long). Ask a child to show b by sliding a finger along the strip.

l7-we3.note: Use 3 real squares (paper or pattern blocks) under the visualiser. Click through the steps. Think-aloud: "I start with all three in a row. Now I move one end square up, so it sits on top of its neighbour: an L. What if I move the middle square up? Then it only touches at corners: not allowed. If I turn the L or flip it over, it is the same L, just turned. So with 3 squares there are only 2 shapes." Let children try to find a third one with their own squares: every try is a line or an L. The Think harder slide asks the same question with 4 squares.

l7-challenge.note: For any pair that chooses Go further. Use it as a pair choice, or with volunteers in talk time (never call a child by name). Ask for the reason every time. Q3 is open: there is no single right answer, so ask children to check each other's work. Answers: 1) 15 triangles with 4 lines and 21 with 5 lines. The number added grows by 1 each time: 3, 6, 10, 15, 21 (+3, +4, +5, +6). Check by drawing: count the small triangles first, then the bigger ones made of 2, 3 … small ones. 2) 9 (1 big, 4 medium, 4 tiny). 3) Open. Check by counting small triangles first, then bigger ones made of 2, 3 … small ones. Example: one line from the top corner to the bottom gives 3 triangles; two lines give 6.

l7-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Reveal one answer at a time and ask a child to explain before you click. Many children stop at one answer: ask "Is there another way?" and "How do you know you found them all?" For Q3, ask two pairs to swap puzzles and solve each other's.

l7-talk.note: Minutes 72 to 79. Pairs talk for 2 minutes. Then ask for volunteers first ("Who would like to share?"), never call a child by name to answer, and say that passing is always fine. No tallies and no rankings. Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Answer: 8 triangles (4 small ones, plus 4 bigger ones each made of 2 small triangles). Count the small ones first, then the pairs.

l7-exit.note: Minutes 79 to 85. Answer: 6 corners; it is a hexagon (the same number of corners as sides). This replaces the 14-squares grid, which is a hard ending for the lesson. Extension: how many squares are in a 3 by 3 grid? (14: 9 + 4 + 1).

l7-reflect.note: Minutes 85 to 88 (3 minutes, after the exit ticket). Children tick or write the Look-back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share their boxes. Praise the strategy ("Drawing it got you unstuck"), not the speed. The "Next time I will try" row is optional and is never marked; at the start of the next lesson the tutor may say, to the whole group, "Today you could try drawing it, using objects or checking your answer" without naming anyone. Say: "Tick what was hard and what helped you. Write or draw one thing you did well. Then tick one thing you might try next time, if you like. You can pass." After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time: the buffer. If the lesson ran late, finish whatever is still open (stamps, the look-back). If you are on time, say goodbye and thank the parents. Do not start anything new.
